newsitem.title: USA: US House encryption-export bill to get smooth ride.
newsitem.headline: US House encryption-export bill to get smooth ride.

text.p: A bill to relax U.S. export limits on computer-encoding technology will be passed with few changes by a House subcommittee this week, the subcommittee's chairwoman said on Monday.
The House International Relations' economic policy and trade subcommittee will vote on the bill on Tuesday, chairwoman Ileana Ros-Lehtinen, Republican of Florida, said.
Current U.S. law strictly limits export of encryption software, which scrambles information and renders it unreadable without a password or software "key."
Once the realm of spies and generals, encryption has become a critical technology to safeguard electronic commerce and global communications over the Internet.
In the Senate last week, a similiar bill to relax encryption-export controls was torpedoed when the Senate Commerce Committee approved a substitute.

The substitute bill, sponsored by Nebraska Democrat Bob Kerrey and Arizona Republican John McCain, would only modestly ease export restrictions and would effectively allow the government to crack encrypted messages in the United States by gaining access to the software keys.

The bill could face a more difficult challenge when considered by the full International Relations Committee. Chairman Benjamin Gilman, Republican of New York, is not a strong supporter of export liberalization, congressional staffers said.
U.S. software companies such as Netscape Communications Corp Microsoft Corp have been clamoring for relief from encryption-export controls.
The heads of 10 software companies, including Microsoft Chairman Bill Gates, came to Washington earlier this month to lobby the Clinton administration for liberalization.

They pointed out that as a result of U.S. controls, foreign companies are gaining market share for encryption products. Sun Microsystems said last month it would evade the rules by marketing Russian-made software with its products.
